seo.title: 36 Interior Design Logos Explained
seo.description: 36 interior design logos explained by a brand designer: studios like Kelly Wearstler and Studio McGee, furniture brands like Vitra and Knoll, design marketplaces and lighting brands.

intro:
The best interior design logos are quiet wordmarks that let the work speak. An interior designer sells taste, so most top studios use the founder's name in a refined typeface and almost no colour. The ones you remember add one confident detail: Kelly Wearstler's extra-wide capitals, Article's coral full stop or Commune's deep red.

What makes a good interior design logo?

Type that matches your style: a classic serif says traditional and luxurious, a light sans serif says modern and calm, and heavy condensed letters say bold and dramatic.

Restraint: clients hire you for your eye, so a simple, well-spaced name builds more trust than a drawing of a sofa or a house.

One ownable detail: a full stop, a monogram, a box or a single colour makes a plain name recognisable.

Works on materials: the logo has to look right embossed on a folder, printed on fabric tags and tiny on Instagram.

Below are 36 logos in four groups: interior design studios, furniture brands, design marketplaces and services, and paint, materials and lighting brands. Each logo has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation. For more ideas, see my luxury real estate branding guide, my fashion logos and my guide to choosing a logo font.

logoResearch.name: Kelly Wearstler
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kelly Wearstler founded her Los Angeles studio in 1995.
observations: Heavy, extra-wide capitals set the full name on one line.
The bold, confident type matches a designer known for daring, sculptural interiors.

logoResearch.name: Studio McGee
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Shea and Syd McGee founded Studio McGee in Utah in 2014.
observations: Thin, widely spaced capitals feel light and calm.
A small raised c in McGee is the one detail that makes the wordmark feel custom.

logoResearch.name: Yabu Pushelberg
logoResearch.verifiedFact: George Yabu and Glenn Pushelberg founded the studio in Toronto in 1980.
observations: Rounded lowercase letters make two long surnames feel soft and friendly.
The logo uses only the founders' names, which suits a studio known for its partners.

logoResearch.name: Rockwell Group
logoResearch.verifiedFact: David Rockwell founded Rockwell Group in New York in 1984.
observations: Heavy lowercase letters run the two words together.
Joining rockwell and group into one word makes the name read like a single mark.

logoResearch.name: Pierre Yovanovitch
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pierre Yovanovitch opened his Paris studio in 2001 after working in fashion with Pierre Cardin.
observations: The logo is just his initials, P and Y, in heavy geometric capitals.
A wide gap between the two letters gives the monogram space, like a gallery wall.

logoResearch.name: India Mahdavi
logoResearch.verifiedFact: India Mahdavi opened her studio in Paris in 1999.
observations: A clean lowercase sans serif sets her first and last name.
The plain type lets her colourful interiors and furniture do the talking.

logoResearch.name: Ken Fulk
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ken Fulk runs a design and events studio based in San Francisco.
observations: Tall, condensed capitals look like a theatre poster.
Tight spacing makes the short name feel bold and dramatic.

logoResearch.name: Commune Design
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Commune was founded in Los Angeles in 2004 by Roman Alonso, Steven Johanknecht and siblings Pamela and Ramin Shamshiri.
observations: A deep red lowercase wordmark is the only colour among the studio logos.
Round, repeating letters give the word commune a warm, communal rhythm.

logoResearch.name: Workstead
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Robert Highsmith and Stefanie Brechbuehler founded Workstead in Brooklyn in 2009.
observations: Tall, condensed capitals feel like signage on an old workshop.
One heavy word, with no symbol, suits a studio known for craft and lighting.

logoResearch.name: RH
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Restoration Hardware was founded in Eureka, California, in 1979 and now trades as RH.
observations: Two tall serif capitals with very thin and very thick strokes.
The high contrast makes two letters look as expensive as a fashion house.

logoResearch.name: West Elm
logoResearch.verifiedFact: West Elm opened in Brooklyn in 2002 and is owned by Williams-Sonoma.
observations: Light lowercase letters are spaced widely.
The relaxed, airy type matches mid-century style furniture for city apartments.

logoResearch.name: CB2
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Crate & Barrel launched CB2 in Chicago in 2000.
observations: Wide capitals sit inside a thin rectangular box.
The box works like a label, which suits a brand born as a spin-off.

logoResearch.name: Article
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Article was founded in Vancouver in 2013 and sells furniture online.
observations: Widely spaced grey capitals feel calm and modern.
A coral full stop is the only colour and turns a common word into a brand.

logoResearch.name: HAY
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rolf and Mette Hay founded HAY in Copenhagen in 2002.
observations: Three heavy black capitals make one of the shortest names here.
The plain, bold type lets colourful products carry the personality.

logoResearch.name: Vitra
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Vitra was founded in Switzerland in 1950 and produces designs by Charles and Ray Eames.
observations: Bold lowercase letters end with a full stop.
The heavy, compact word feels engineered, which fits a company known for chairs.

logoResearch.name: Knoll
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Knoll was founded in New York in 1938 and is now part of MillerKnoll.
observations: Very heavy letters in orange-red are set tightly together.
The strong colour makes the short name stand out in showrooms and catalogues.

logoResearch.name: Herman Miller
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The company took the name Herman Miller in Zeeland, Michigan, in 1923 and is now part of MillerKnoll.
observations: A bold red M symbol sits before the name.
The full name in the same red joins the two words without a space.

logoResearch.name: Design Within Reach
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rob Forbes founded Design Within Reach in 1998, and it is now part of MillerKnoll.
observations: White initials sit at the bottom of a solid black square.
The DWR box works as a stamp on catalogues, stores and shopping bags.

logoResearch.name: Houzz
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Adi Tatarko and Alon Cohen founded Houzz in Palo Alto in 2009.
observations: A green h mark is shaped like a simple house.
Rounded lowercase letters make the platform feel friendly and approachable.

logoResearch.name: Havenly
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Lee Mayer and Emily Motayed founded Havenly in Denver in 2014.
observations: Thin, wide serif capitals look elegant and traditional.
The classic type makes an online service feel like a high-end studio.

logoResearch.name: Decorilla
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Decorilla is an online interior design service that matches clients with designers.
observations: A square mark looks like a window frame or a floor plan.
Thin capitals beside it keep the logo clean and light.

logoResearch.name: 1stDibs
logoResearch.verifiedFact: 1stDibs started in 2001 as an online catalogue of dealers at the Paris flea market.
observations: A stacked st sits beside the 1, like a raised ordinal on an old price tag.
Classic serif capitals suit a marketplace for antiques and luxury design.

logoResearch.name: Chairish
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Anna and Gregg Brockway founded Chairish in San Francisco in 2013.
observations: A red brush script spells the name with a long swash on the h.
The handwriting style makes a marketplace feel personal, like a shop owner's sign.

logoResearch.name: Wayfair
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Niraj Shah and Steve Conine founded the company in Boston in 2002.
observations: A purple pinwheel mark sits before the name.
Rounded lowercase letters in the same purple make the brand feel friendly and mass-market.

logoResearch.name: Burrow
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Burrow was founded in New York in 2017 and sells modular sofas online.
observations: Wide, geometric grey capitals feel calm and modern.
The round letters echo soft furniture shapes.

logoResearch.name: Floyd
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Floyd was founded in Detroit in 2014, starting with a table leg that clamps onto any surface.
observations: Heavy black capitals make the short name feel solid.
The industrial type suits a brand built around simple, sturdy furniture.

logoResearch.name: Lulu and Georgia
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sara Sugarman founded Lulu and Georgia in Los Angeles in 2012.
observations: Widely spaced capitals set the two names far apart.
A tiny AND tied with a small red bow sits between them.

logoResearch.name: Tom Dixon
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tom Dixon launched his own design brand in London in 2002.
observations: The name is stacked in heavy, slightly quirky letters.
A full stop at the end gives the logo a confident, final feel.

logoResearch.name: Benjamin Moore
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Benjamin Moore was founded in Brooklyn in 1883 and is owned by Berkshire Hathaway.
observations: A black triangle with an M inside sits before the name.
Bold sans serif letters make the paint brand easy to read on cans and in stores.

logoResearch.name: Sherwin-Williams
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sherwin-Williams was founded in Cleveland in 1866.
observations: Blue italic capitals lean forward over two lines.
The wordmark is often paired with the brand's Cover the Earth globe.

logoResearch.name: Schumacher
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Frederic Schumacher founded the fabric house in New York in 1889.
observations: Classic serif capitals are spaced evenly across the name.
The traditional type suits a brand known for archive wallpapers and fabrics.

logoResearch.name: Flos
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Flos was founded in Merano, Italy, in 1962.
observations: Tall, thin serif capitals with very fine details.
Four letters look like they were drawn with a light, precise pen, which suits a lighting brand.

logoResearch.name: Louis Poulsen
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Louis Poulsen was founded in Copenhagen in 1874 and is known for Poul Henningsen's PH lamps.
observations: Heavy lowercase letters set both words close together.
The rounded letters feel warm, like the glow of its lamps.

logoResearch.name: Artemide
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ernesto Gismondi and Sergio Mazza founded Artemide in Milan in 1960.
observations: A heavy red slab serif makes the name bold and dramatic.
The strong colour and weight stand out among quieter design brands.

logoResearch.name: Kvadrat
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kvadrat was founded in Ebeltoft, Denmark, in 1968.
observations: Heavy lowercase letters make one solid word.
The name means square in Danish, and the compact block of letters echoes it.

logoResearch.name: Fireclay Tile
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Fireclay Tile was founded in California in 1986 and makes tile from recycled materials.
observations: A square mark divided into tiles sits before the name.
The name is stacked in two lines of spaced capitals next to the mark.

listIntro: The boards below show all 36 interior design logos in one consistent format, grouped into studios, furniture brands, marketplaces and services, and paint, materials and lighting.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the quality of the interiors or products behind it.
sectionIntroductions: Top interior design studios use the founder's name and very little else. The personality comes from the typeface: extra-wide capitals for Kelly Wearstler, soft lowercase for Yabu Pushelberg and condensed capitals for Workstead.
Furniture brands range from luxury serifs like RH to bold, compact wordmarks like HAY, Vitra and Knoll that work on labels, tags and catalogues.
Online design services and marketplaces need to feel friendly and trustworthy on a screen, so they use rounded letters, a simple symbol or a personal script like Chairish.
Paint, fabric and lighting brands are some of the oldest names here, and their logos mix heritage serifs like Schumacher with bold, modern marks like Artemide and Kvadrat.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of interior design logos, not a ranking of designers or products.
Look at how each logo uses type, spacing and one detail to signal luxury, warmth or modern simplicity.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a proposal, a fabric tag and an Instagram profile.

findings.heading: Names beat symbols
findings.text: Almost every studio uses the founder's name or initials. Clients hire a person's taste, so the name is the brand.

findings.heading: Typeface sets the style
findings.text: Serifs like RH, Schumacher and Havenly feel classic and luxurious. Light sans serifs like West Elm and Studio McGee feel calm and modern.

findings.heading: Colour is rare and powerful
findings.text: Commune's red, Knoll's orange-red, Herman Miller's red and Article's coral dot stand out because most interior brands are black or grey.

findings.heading: Short names win
findings.text: RH, HAY, CB2 and DWR shorten long names to a few letters that work on tags, boxes and storefronts.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for an interior design logo
checklistItems: Does the typeface match the style of your interiors?
Is it simple enough to emboss, foil or print on fabric tags?
Is there one detail you can own, like a monogram, a colour or a full stop?
Does it avoid clichés like houses, sofas and lamps?
Will it read small on Instagram and large on a showroom wall?

faq.question: What makes a good interior design logo?
faq.answer: A good interior design logo is a refined wordmark with one memorable detail. The typeface should match the style of your interiors, and the logo should work embossed, printed on fabric and small on social media.

faq.question: What fonts are best for an interior design logo?
faq.answer: Classic serifs suit traditional and luxury interiors, light sans serifs suit modern and minimal work, and condensed capitals suit bold, dramatic styles. Keep it to one typeface and space it generously.

faq.question: Should an interior design logo include a symbol?
faq.answer: It is optional. Most leading studios use only a name or initials. If you add a symbol, keep it simple, like a monogram, and avoid houses, sofas and lamps.

faq.question: What colours work for an interior design logo?
faq.answer: Black, grey and deep neutrals are the most common because they sit well next to any interior. One signature colour, like Commune's red or Article's coral dot, can make a simple logo memorable.

faq.question: How much does an interior design logo cost?
faq.answer: Prices range from a few hundred dollars for a template to tens of thousands with a large agency. I design a complete brand identity in one week for a flat $3,000, including the logo, colours, typography and guidelines.
